Editing a rule set stages it. The running firewall changes only when you apply, and only stays changed if you confirm inside the acceptance window.
That is what makes a mistake recoverable: lose your connection and the previous rules come back on their own.
Put your own management address on the {}. It survives a closed SSH port and every protection module.
Ports that accept inbound connections on every interface.
No {{.Type}} port is open. Add one to accept inbound connections.
A single port is `443`. A contiguous range is `8000:9000`, written with a colon.
Every rule here applies to all interfaces. To restrict a source address, use the {} or a {}.
Marking a rule applies the SSH brute-force limiter to it, so repeated connection attempts from one address get rate-limited.
The limiter itself is switched on under {}. Without it, the mark has no effect.
Sources that are dropped before any other rule is evaluated.
Nothing from these sources reaches an open port.
One per line — IPv4, IPv6 or CIDR. A line starting with `#` is a comment.
Accepted forms: a single address `192.0.2.42`, a network `198.51.100.0/24`, or IPv6 in either form.
The blacklist is evaluated first. An address listed here is dropped even if a port rule would have accepted it.
This list is evaluated *before* the {}. An address that appears in both is dropped — a narrow allow inside a wide block does not work.
Trusted sources that reach every port, including ports you never opened.
Accepted before the port rules are consulted, and exempt from the protection modules.
Use it as your way back in
Your own management address belongs here. It keeps you reachable even if a port rule closes SSH or a rate limit trips.
A whitelisted source skips the port rules entirely, so it reaches services that are not listed under {} at all.
An entry here bypasses every protection module. Prefer a single address over a range, and a range over a whole network.
The {} is evaluated first: an address in both lists is dropped, not allowed.
Redirect traffic arriving on one port to another port on this host.
Nothing is being redirected. Add a rule to forward a port.
A rule sends traffic that arrives on the incoming port to the destination port on this same host — `8080 → 80` means a request to 8080 is served by whatever listens on 80.

The *destination* port is the one that has to be open, not the incoming one: the redirect happens before the filter sees the packet, so by then it is addressed to the destination port. Open it under {}.
Redirecting a privileged port to a high one is the usual way to run a service without root. Check that nothing else already holds the destination port.
Raw nftables rules, applied after everything easywall generates itself.
One statement per line, inserted into the `inet easywall` table.

# Example: allow a specific port
tcp dport 8443 accept

# Allow traffic from specific IP
ip saddr 203.0.113.1 accept
Nothing here is validated against your intent — only against nftables syntax. The {} is what protects you: if a rule cuts your connection, not confirming restores the previous set.
Write the rule body only. easywall prefixes each line with `add rule inet easywall input`, so every statement lands in the input chain.
Write `tcp dport 8443 accept` — not the full `add rule` command.
Protection modules that apply to every interface. An accent edge marks a module that is on.

Address families and container networks the firewall has to account for.
Whether the inet table filters IPv6, and which discovery messages get through.
Discard all IPv6 except loopback. For hosts that have no business speaking IPv6 at all.
Accept all IPv6 before any rule is consulted. Only for hosts where something else — an upstream firewall, a cloud security group — is already filtering IPv6.
Every rule applies to IPv6 as well as IPv4, and the ICMPv6 types IPv6 needs are permitted. The right choice for almost every host.
The table is `inet`, so this decides whether IPv6 goes through the same rules, past them, or nowhere.
Accept ICMPv6 types 133 and 134. Needed for stateless address autoconfiguration on most networks.
Accept ICMPv6 types 135 and 136, the IPv6 equivalent of an ARP request and reply.
Container bridges use private ranges that the bogon filter would otherwise drop.
Look up the bridge networks Docker has created on this host.
Accept traffic from every detected bridge CIDR. Without this, detection alone changes nothing.
One CIDR per line. These are always allowed, whether or not detection finds them.
Saved immediately. Rule changes stay staged until you {}.
This used to be a switch, and it lied

Before 2.5.0 there was an on/off toggle whose *off* position was documented as leaving IPv6 unfiltered. It did the opposite: every rule still applied, and only the ICMPv6 exemptions were removed, so IPv6 ended up filtered and broken. Existing configurations were moved to *Filter it*.
Docker writes its own nftables rules. easywall allows the bridge ranges before the blacklist, so container traffic keeps working.
Bridges are detected when rules are applied. A network created afterwards needs a new apply, or an entry above.
What happens to traffic this host passes on rather than receives — between two interfaces, or out of a container.
Nothing is passed on except what Docker coexistence allows. The right answer for a plain server, which routes nothing anyway.
Traffic with a source or a destination in one of the networks below is passed on. Everything else is not.
easywall stops having an opinion about what is passed on and filters only what arrives for this host. For a router whose far side keeps changing.
One CIDR per line. Read only under *Route these networks*.
Why this needs saying at all
easywall's forward chain drops by default, and a drop there is final — a rule elsewhere that accepts the same packet does not save it. So a host that routes has to say so here.
Docker's networks cross regardless of this setting. Turning coexistence on is already that statement.
The safety net that gets you back in when a rule change goes wrong.
After an apply, easywall waits for you to confirm. No confirmation, and the previous rules come back.
Do not switch this off on a remote host
Without the acceptance window an apply is final. A rule that closes your own SSH port leaves you with no way back in short of console access.
Long enough to open a second connection and test what you changed. Short enough that a lockout resolves itself before it costs you the afternoon.
120 seconds suits most cases. Raise it if your check involves more than an SSH login.
A critical fix matters differently at ten installations and at ten thousand. Counting is the only way to tell which this is — and whether a fix has reached most of them.

Once a day, a random identifier generated on this machine and the version easywall is running. Not the hostname, not an address, not a rule, not a count of anything you have configured. Switch it off and the next day nothing is sent; the identifier lives in your data directory and can be deleted.
Push the staged rules to the kernel, then confirm they work before the window closes.
The new rules are live but unconfirmed. Open a second connection and check that you can still reach this host — then confirm.
The rules are confirmed and stay in place.
The window closed without a confirmation, so the previous rules were restored. Nothing you staged was lost — review it and apply again.
You have staged changes that the running firewall does not have yet.
The running firewall matches what is staged. There is nothing to apply.
Staged changes are waiting. They do nothing until you apply them.
Rules were rolled back — acceptance timeout.
The staged set is pushed to the kernel immediately and starts filtering traffic.
Open a *second* connection — keep the current one — and confirm SSH and your services still answer.
Confirming keeps the new rules. Doing nothing restores the previous set when the window closes, which is what saves you if you just locked yourself out.
How long you get before an unconfirmed apply is rolled back is set under {}.
Short enough that a lockout resolves itself quickly; long enough to actually test. The default is 120 seconds.
The password for signing in to this interface. You stay signed in on this device after changing it.
Hashed with Argon2id and a per-password salt. The plain value is never written anywhere, which also means it cannot be recovered — only replaced.
There is no reset link — this interface sends no mail and reaches no outside service. Recovery means editing the web config on the host itself.
